content: Burdock refers to a group of biennial thistles belonging to the genus Arctium in the family Asteraceae. Common burdock (Arctium minus) is widely distributed across North America, Europe, and Asia. The plants in this genus have dark green leaves that can grow up to 18 inches (45 cm) in length. These leaves are typically large, coarse, and ovate, with the lower leaves being heart-shaped. The undersides of the leaves are woolly, and the leafstalks are generally hollow. Species of Arctium typically flower between July and October. The plants are known for their prickly seed heads, which easily attach to fur and clothing, serving as an effective mechanism for seed dispersal. These burrs can cause local irritation and, in some cases, intestinal hairballs in pets, although most animals tend to avoid consuming the plant. Over time, many species initially classified under the genus Arctium have been reclassified into the related genus Cousinia. The distinction between Arctium and Cousinia is challenging to define, as their molecular phylogenies are closely correlated. Burdock is sometimes mistaken for cockleburs (Xanthium) or rhubarb (Rheum). The roots of burdock serve as a food source for the larvae of the ghost moth (Hepialus humuli), and the plant is also utilized by other Lepidoptera species, including the brown-tail moth, Coleophora paripennella, Coleophora peribenanderi, the gothic moth, lime-speck pug, and scalloped hazel. The green, above-ground parts of the plant can cause contact dermatitis in humans due to the lactones it produces. Food and Drink The taproot of young burdock plants can be harvested and consumed as a root vegetable. While it is not commonly used in modern European cuisine, it remains popular in Asia, particularly in Japan, where Arctium lappa (greater burdock) is known as gobō (牛蒡 or ゴボウ). The plant is cultivated for its long, slender roots, which can grow up to 1 meter in length and 2 cm in diameter. Burdock root is crisp and has a sweet, mild, and slightly pungent flavor, with a hint of earthy harshness that can be reduced by soaking julienned or shredded roots in water for 5–10 minutes. Immature flower stalks can also be harvested in late spring before the flowers bloom, and their flavor is similar to that of artichokes, a related plant. In Japanese cuisine, burdock is featured in dishes such as kinpira gobō (julienned burdock root and carrot braised with soy sauce, sugar, mirin, sake, and sesame oil) and burdock makizushi (sushi rolls filled with pickled burdock root, often dyed orange to resemble carrots). In the latter half of the 20th century, burdock gained international recognition due to the popularity of the macrobiotic diet, which advocates its consumption. Burdock root is a good source of dietary fiber (6 g per 100 g), calcium, potassium, amino acids, and is low in calories. It also contains polyphenols, which can cause the root's surface to darken and contribute to its earthy harshness. However, this flavor pairs well with pork in dishes like miso soup (tonjiru) and Japanese-style pilaf (takikomi gohan). In the United Kingdom, burdock is a key ingredient in the traditional soft drink dandelion and burdock. Additionally, burdock is believed to act as a galactagogue, a substance that promotes lactation. Traditional Medicine In folk medicine, dried burdock is considered a diuretic, diaphoretic, and blood purifier. The seeds of Arctium lappa are used in traditional Chinese medicine under the name niupangzi (牛蒡子). Burdock has been used as a traditional medicinal herb for various ailments. Burdock root oil extract, also known as bur oil, is widely used in Europe as a scalp treatment. It is believed to improve hair strength, shine, and body, as well as to address scalp conditions such as dandruff and hair loss. Modern research has shown that burdock root oil extract is rich in phytosterols and essential fatty acids, including rare long-chain EFAs, which are essential for maintaining a healthy scalp and promoting natural hair growth. The oil provides immediate relief while supporting the normal function of sebaceous glands and hair follicles. Some European herbalists recommend combining burdock root oil with nettle root oil and massaging the mixture into the scalp daily for enhanced effects. Burdock and Velcro In the early 1940s, Swiss inventor George de Mestral became intrigued by the burdock seeds that clung to his clothes and his dog's fur after a walk. Upon examining the seeds under a microscope, he observed their hook-and-loop structure, which allows them to attach to passing animals for seed dispersal. This observation inspired him to develop Velcro, a fastening system based on the same principle. Tolstoy's Reflection The Russian writer Leo Tolstoy mentioned burdock in his journal in 1896. He described seeing a small burdock shoot in a ploughed field, black from dust but still alive and red in the center. He reflected on its resilience and vitality, which inspired him to write, as the plant symbolized life persisting against all odds. Species Arctium lappa: Greater Burdock, Gobō Arctium minus: Lesser Burdock, Burweed, Louse-bur, Button-bur Arctium minus nemorosum (syn. Arctium vulgare): Woodland Burdock, Wood Burdock Arctium pubens: Common Burdock Arctium tomentosum: Downy Burdock, Woolly Burdock Safety The roots of burdock closely resemble those of deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna), a highly toxic plant. This similarity poses a risk of contamination in burdock preparations. It is essential to purchase burdock products from reputable companies and to avoid gathering burdock in the wild unless you are confident in your ability to correctly identify the plant.
